A savings forecast needs a sensitivity check: read the range behind the ranking

Use a tornado chart, a deposit curve, a two-input matrix and a combined-case bridge to see which authored assumptions move a future funding gap.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Test the saving-gap assumptions individually and together

Interactive planning lab

Modeled project price at the payment date$60,832.65
Modeled signed gap: price less available savings$16,949.42
Month-end deposit needed to close this baseline gap$762.45

Original deterministic nominal-CAD saving illustration. The project price grows at the entered constant annual rate. Starting savings and equal month-end deposits earn a constant effective annual return converted to a monthly rate; negative rates are allowed, but no uncertain return path is simulated. The full project bill is paid at the end of the selected whole-year period, with no earlier deposits to suppliers. A positive gap means a shortfall and a negative gap excess savings relative to this modeled bill. No tax, fees, borrowing, reserve earmark or guarantee is included. The sensitivity chart changes one input at a time: quote ± the selected percentage; monthly saving ±25%; return and price growth ±2 percentage points, bounded to their stated baseline ranges; and the deadline ±1 year, bounded to 1–15 years. Quotes and deposits are scaled stress cases, so their tested endpoints may exceed baseline form limits. All tested inputs are listed in the data table. Ranges are authored assumptions, not confidence intervals, probability distributions, equally likely outcomes or a global sensitivity decomposition. The combined case applies its five changes together in the stated order, without calling it a worst case.

The central idea

A sensitivity ranking depends on the input ranges you test. Changing one assumption at a time does not describe every joint outcome or assign probabilities to the results.

01

Choose the planning question before ranking the inputs

A projection can display a future balance to the nearest cent while its price, saving and return assumptions remain uncertain. Extra decimal places do not make those assumptions more reliable. A useful next step is to ask how the result changes when a specific assumption moves over a stated range.

This illustration asks about a signed funding gap: the project bill at the payment date less the savings available then. A positive gap means the modeled bill is not fully funded; a negative gap means savings exceed it. That output combines the cost of the goal with the assets intended to fund it, rather than focusing on the investment balance alone.

The default project costs CAD 50,000 today and grows at an assumed 4% annually for five years. Starting savings are CAD 10,000, with CAD 500 deposited at each month-end and a constant assumed 3% effective annual return. The future bill is about CAD 60,832.65, savings about CAD 43,883.22, and the gap about CAD 16,949.42.

02

Read the tornado chart as a set of one-input experiments

Each row changes one assumption while holding every other baseline input fixed. The tested quote is 20% lower or higher by default. Monthly deposits are 25% lower or higher. Savings return and project-price growth move two percentage points either side, subject to their stated bounds. The deadline moves one year earlier or later, within one to fifteen years.

The first chart expresses every result in the same output unit: CAD change from the baseline gap. Its pale bar connects the two tested changes. A filled marker identifies the lower input, and an open marker the higher input. The original input values and their units remain in the data table.

“Lower input” is not shorthand for “better outcome.” Reducing the project quote reduces the gap; reducing monthly saving increases it. Likewise, an earlier deadline changes the number of deposits, the savings-growth period and the project-price growth period simultaneously. The sign of its effect depends on the selected amounts.

03

A wide tested range can make an input appear more influential

The rows are ordered by the absolute difference between the two tested output changes. At the defaults, the CAD 40,000 and CAD 60,000 quote cases move the future gap by roughly minus and plus CAD 12,166.53. The CAD 375 and CAD 625 monthly-saving cases move it by roughly plus and minus CAD 8,072.62.

The quote therefore appears above monthly saving for these chosen ranges. That does not establish a universal ranking of quote risk over saving discipline. Change the quote-range control to zero, and that row has no tested spread because both quote endpoints equal the baseline. Its rank changes even though the underlying saving formula is unchanged.

The controls and fixed ranges are original teaching choices, not confidence intervals, equally likely cases or measured error margins. A ranking has practical meaning only when the ranges themselves are defensible for the decision. A firm quote, an uncertain estimate and a voluntary deposit commitment may deserve different evidence and different ranges.

04

Use the deposit curve to distinguish a controllable amount from a forecast

The deposit curve changes only the month-end saving amount. At the defaults, a deposit of about CAD 762.45 per month closes the modeled gap. That is an algebraic threshold under the constant return, price-growth and payment-date assumptions.

It is not a guarantee that this contribution will fund an actual project. The project price can differ, returns can vary, deposits can be missed and earlier supplier payments may be required. Nor does the calculation establish that the household can afford that monthly commitment. The take-home budget and other savings goals still need to be checked.

HM Treasury’s 2026 Green Book describes sensitivity testing and switching values as ways to examine how changed assumptions affect an appraisal. This guide applies that broad analytical idea to an original household illustration; it does not import UK public-sector appraisal rules or discount rates into a personal saving recommendation.

05

A single-input chart leaves combinations unexplored

The return-and-deadline matrix changes two inputs together. Each cell recomputes the future bill, savings and signed gap at its specified horizon and return, with the other selected baseline inputs retained. A five-year 3% cell matches the default baseline when the other inputs remain at their defaults.

The European Commission Joint Research Centre’s methods discussion distinguishes one-factor-at-a-time approaches from methods that examine input combinations and interactions. An interaction can occur when the effect of changing two inputs differs from the sum of their separate effects.

In this model, price growth acts on the project quote for the selected number of years, while savings returns act on both starting money and later deposits. Those relationships can make combined effects differ from the isolated changes shown in the tornado chart. The small matrix exposes selected combinations; it is not a complete global sensitivity analysis.

06

Reconcile a combined case without adding isolated effects as if they were bills

The final bridge applies the higher tested quote, higher price growth, lower monthly saving, lower return and earlier deadline together. At the defaults, the combined case uses a CAD 60,000 current quote, 6% price growth, CAD 375 monthly saving, a 1% return and four years. Its modeled funding gap is about CAD 46,987.18.

Adding those five separate one-input gap changes to the baseline would instead give about CAD 50,737.62. The difference is not missing money. The isolated effects each started from the original baseline, while the combined case changes interacting inputs together.

The bridge uses a fixed sequence to reconcile the actual combined result. Each step measures the change after all previous steps have already occurred. Reordering the steps can change their individual amounts while preserving the same final combined case. The steps are therefore an accounting explanation of this chosen path, not a unique allocation of causation to each input.

This case is not labelled a global worst outcome. In particular, moving the deadline earlier is not necessarily the most adverse change under every set of price and saving assumptions. No likelihood is attached to the combined endpoint.

07

Use sensitivity to direct the next evidence check

  1. Define the output that matters, such as the funding gap at a specific payment date.
  2. Write the baseline timing, units and cash-flow assumptions.
  3. Choose evidence-based ranges and keep the tested endpoints inspectable.
  4. Review important combinations after the one-input comparison.
  5. Separate what the household can change from what needs contingency funding.

A large sensitivity can indicate where a better quote, a firmer date or a revised saving commitment would improve the plan. A small sensitivity over a narrow chosen range is not proof that an assumption is certain. The method helps organise further work; it does not replace uncertainty evidence, an affordability review or a dated cash plan.

The model excludes tax, fees, borrowing, earmarked emergency reserves and uncertain return paths. It assumes the entire bill arrives at the final date. A project with staged payments needs its actual calendar before this end-date funding comparison is used.
